Monte Carlo Sensitivity Analysis for Minimum Risk Point Estimation

Source: R/sensitivity_mr.R
seq_mr_sensitivity.Rd

These functions run a minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) procedure from its pilot sample to its stopping point G times, on data simulated from a population whose true value is known, and summarize what happened: how many observations the procedure took compared with the best fixed sample size, and how the realized risk compares with the risk of that best fixed design. Use them before collecting data, to see what a choice of the loss constant A and the sampling cost c implies, and to see how the procedure behaves when checking in batches or when the population is not the one the method assumes.

Usage

seq_mr_cv_sensitivity(
  true_value,
  A,
  c,
  distribution = c("gamma", "lognormal", "normal"),
  variance = c("corrected", "published"),
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  gamma = 0.49,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

seq_mr_smd_sensitivity(
  true_value,
  A,
  c,
  distribution = c("normal", "skewed"),
  G = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  m_0 = 4,
  gamma = 0.49,
  max_n = 100000L,
  batch = 1L
)

Arguments

true_value

The population value. For the coefficient of variation it must be positive; for the standardized mean difference it must be less than 100 million in absolute value. A value so extreme that the population cannot be generated, or that the benchmark is not a positive finite number, is an error.

A

The loss constant, the price of one unit of squared estimation error. A single positive number.

c

The cost of sampling one observation. A single positive number or, for the standardized mean difference, two positive numbers, c(c1, c2), the cost in each group.

distribution

The population to simulate from. For the coefficient of variation: "gamma" (the default), "lognormal", or "normal" (mean 1), each with coefficient of variation true_value. For the standardized mean difference: "normal" (the default; unit variance in both groups, means true_value and 0) or "skewed" (the same means and variance, with a standardized chi square distribution on 3 degrees of freedom in place of the normal).

variance

For seq_mr_cv_sensitivity(), the variance estimator passed to seq_mr_cv: "corrected" (the default) or "published".

G

The number of Monte Carlo replications: a whole number of at least 2. The default is 1000. The examples use far fewer so that they run quickly; a reported analysis deserves at least the default.

seed

A single whole number that set.seed() accepts, to make the result reproducible, or NULL (the default) to use the current state of the random number generator. When a seed is given, the generator's state is restored afterward.

m_0

The smallest pilot size allowed (per group for the standardized mean difference): a whole number of at least 4, the default.

gamma

The tuning constant of the correction term, strictly between 0 and 1/2; default 0.49.

max_n

A cap on the sample size (on each group's size for the standardized mean difference): a replication that reaches it is stopped there. A whole number no smaller than the pilot size. The cap is exact: the last batch is shortened if needed. The default is large; see "Run time" in Details before using it with constants whose optimal sample size is in the thousands.

batch

The number of observations added between checks of the stopping rule: a whole number of at least 1. The default, 1, is the purely sequential procedure of the articles. For the standardized mean difference it is the number added per group with one cost, and the number added to the less costly group with two costs.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_sensitivity", "data.frame") (see smsd_sensitivity_methods): a data frame with columns term (character) and value (numeric), one row per summary, that prints in fixed notation. The values are stored unrounded. For seq_mr_cv_sensitivity() the rows are

true_value, loss_A, cost, replications

the inputs;

optimal_n, minimum_risk

the benchmark: the best fixed sample size and the risk there;

mean_n, median_n, sd_n

the mean, median, and standard deviation of the final sample size;

ratio_n

mean_n divided by optimal_n;

mean_estimate

the mean of the final estimates;

mean_risk

the mean realized loss;

risk_efficiency

mean_risk divided by minimum_risk;

se_risk_efficiency

the Monte Carlo standard error of risk_efficiency;

regret

mean_risk minus minimum_risk, in the currency of c;

pct_hit_max_n

the percentage (0 to 100) of replications stopped by max_n.

For seq_mr_smd_sensitivity() the rows are the same, except that cost is cost_1 and cost_2, and each sample size row is reported for both groups: optimal_n1, optimal_n2, mean_n1, mean_n2, median_n1, median_n2, sd_n1, sd_n2, ratio_n1, and ratio_n2. A replication stopped by max_n whose final data give no estimate (a sample mean that is not positive, or constant data) is left out of mean_estimate and the four risk rows, which are NA when every replication is left out (pct_hit_max_n is then 100).

Details

The function seq_mr_cv_sensitivity() runs seq_mr_cv (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016), and the function seq_mr_smd_sensitivity() runs seq_mr_smd (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2017). Each replication applies the same stopping rule as the check function, to the same kind of growing sample a user would collect.

What a replication does. It draws the pilot sample (seq_mr_cv_pilot or seq_mr_smd_pilot), evaluates the stopping rule, and, while the rule is not met, adds batch observations and evaluates it again. For the standardized mean difference with one cost, each stage adds batch observations to each group. With two costs it follows the article's order: each stage adds batch observations to the less costly group and then brings the costlier group up to the size the article pairs with it. With batch = 1 these are the sizes seq_mr_smd reports in its rows next_n1 and next_n2, so a replication is the loop that function's help describes. A stage at which the check function would report the rule as not met for want of an estimate (a sample mean that is not positive, constant data, a variance estimate that is zero, negative, or not finite), or at which the criterion is too large to represent, is a stage at which the rule is not met: sampling goes on. The realized loss of a replication is the squared error of its final estimate priced at A, plus what its observations cost.

Run time. The stopping rule is evaluated on all the data collected so far after every batch, so the time for one replication grows faster than its final sample size, and toward the square of it for large samples. On the machine used to check the package, with batch = 1, one replication of the coefficient of variation procedure took about 0.004 seconds at a final sample size near 100, 0.07 seconds near 1,100, and 0.5 seconds near 4,000 (about nine minutes for the default G); batch = 50 brought the last figure to 0.01 seconds. When the optimal sample size is in the thousands, use a larger batch, a smaller G, or a smaller max_n.

The benchmark. optimal_n (or optimal_n1 and optimal_n2) is the fixed sample size that minimizes the large sample risk for the simulated population, and minimum_risk is the risk there. They are not rounded. For the coefficient of variation they are \(n_c = (A\,\xi^2/c)^{1/2}\) and \(2 c\, n_c\) (Equations 15 and 16 of Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016), with \(\xi^2\) the asymptotic variance of the simulated population (Equation 30 of Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018) whichever variance is requested. For the standardized mean difference they minimize the approximate risk of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017, Equation 9, or Equation 17 with two costs). That risk assumes normal populations. For distribution = "skewed" the benchmark instead uses the large sample mean squared error of the estimate for the skewed population, \(1/n_1 + 1/n_2 + 3\delta^2 / \{2(n_1 + n_2)\}\), so that the risk efficiency shows what the normality assumption costs.

Reading the result. A procedure that works as intended has ratio_n and risk_efficiency near 1. Both guarantees are asymptotic (they hold as A / c grows). At small sample sizes the correction term makes the procedure take more than the optimal number of observations (for the standardized mean difference with A = 500 and c = 2, about 19 per group against 16), and for a strongly skewed population the coefficient of variation procedure stops early (for gamma data with a coefficient of variation of 1.3, A = 900, and c = 1, about 26 observations against 45). The benchmark is a large sample approximation, so at small sample sizes risk_efficiency can fall below 1; that reflects the approximation, not a procedure better than the best fixed design. risk_efficiency is also an average of very variable losses, so judge it against se_risk_efficiency. If pct_hit_max_n is above zero, some replications were stopped by max_n and not by the rule, and the other rows are censored.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2017). Estimating the standardized mean difference with minimum risk: Maximizing accuracy and minimizing cost with sequential estimation. Psychological Methods, 22(1), 94–113. doi:10.1037/met0000089

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Examples

# A survey team prices squared error at A = 2,000 and pays 1 per
# respondent. If household spending has a coefficient of variation of
# 0.5, how many respondents will the procedure take?
out <- seq_mr_cv_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, A = 2000, c = 1, G = 100,
                             seed = 113)
out
#> term                value
#> true_value          0.5
#> loss_A              2000
#> cost                1
#> replications        100
#> optimal_n           17.67767
#> minimum_risk        35.35534
#> mean_n              18.3
#> median_n            18
#> sd_n                3.026816
#> ratio_n             1.035204
#> mean_estimate       0.489766
#> mean_risk           36.83699
#> risk_efficiency     1.041908
#> se_risk_efficiency  0.07084226
#> regret              1.481655
#> pct_hit_max_n       0
out$value[out$term == "ratio_n"]
#> [1] 1.035204

# A training study prices squared error at A = 500 and pays 2 per
# participant in each group. For a true standardized mean difference of
# 0.5, checking after every pair of participants:
seq_mr_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, A = 500, c = 2, G = 100,
                       seed = 113)
#> term                value
#> true_value          0.5
#> loss_A              500
#> cost_1              2
#> cost_2              2
#> replications        100
#> optimal_n1          16.05654
#> optimal_n2          16.05654
#> minimum_risk        128.4523
#> mean_n1             19.24
#> mean_n2             19.24
#> median_n1           19
#> median_n2           19
#> sd_n1               0.4739688
#> sd_n2               0.4739688
#> ratio_n1            1.198266
#> ratio_n2            1.198266
#> mean_estimate       0.5115002
#> mean_risk           130.8696
#> risk_efficiency     1.018819
#> se_risk_efficiency  0.0610766
#> regret              2.417313
#> pct_hit_max_n       0

# The control group costs twice as much per participant, and the rule is
# checked after every fifth participant in the less costly group.
seq_mr_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, A = 500, c = c(2, 4), G = 100,
                       seed = 113, batch = 5)
#> term                value
#> true_value          0.5
#> loss_A              500
#> cost_1              2
#> cost_2              4
#> replications        100
#> optimal_n1          16.14988
#> optimal_n2          11.29811
#> minimum_risk        154.9844
#> mean_n1             22.15
#> mean_n2             13.03
#> median_n1           22
#> median_n2           13
#> sd_n1               0.857233
#> sd_n2               0.1714466
#> ratio_n1            1.371528
#> ratio_n2            1.15329
#> mean_estimate       0.5792
#> mean_risk           182.6061
#> risk_efficiency     1.178222
#> se_risk_efficiency  0.08753002
#> regret              27.62165
#> pct_hit_max_n       0
